**Before running:** Ensure that `cleaned data.Rda` has been generated by running `cleaned_data.Rmd` and is saved in the same directory as this Rmd file.

**Viewing results:** Knit this file to HTML for easier viewing of formatted regression tables, equations and explanations. Individual code chunks can also be executed directly in RStudio.

# 1. Research objective and specification

We estimate the immigrant-sounding name penalty in employer callback rates and test whether it differs by three pre-specified moderators: language skills, extracurricular activities, and multinational firm experience. The regression estimates provide a theory-driven counterpart to the causal forest's subgroup treatment-effect estimates.

| Moderator (X) | Variable | Research question | Expected interaction |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Language skills | `language_skills` | Does listing language proficiency reduce the immigrant-name callback penalty? | Positive |
| Extracurricular activities | `extracurricular_skills` | Do extracurricular signals reduce the immigrant-name callback penalty? | Positive |
| Multinational firm experience | `same_exp` | Does multinational firm experience reduce the immigrant-name callback penalty? | Positive |

The interaction hypotheses are motivated by statistical discrimination theory: additional resume signals may reduce employer uncertainty about applicant productivity.

The regressions are estimated separately for each moderator, using the waves in which that characteristic was randomized. Language skills and extracurricular activities use Waves 0, 1 and 2, while multinational firm experience uses Waves 0 and 1 due to structural missingness in Wave 2.

All regressions include wave fixed effects and firm-clustered CR2 standard errors. Control variables are selected according to the principle of retaining only variables observed across all waves included in each regression. 

# 2. Setup and data preparation

The analysis uses the cleaned Type 0/1 sample (`df_int1`) also used in the balance-table and causal-forest scripts. Treatment `D = 1` denotes an immigrant-sounding name (Type 1), and `D = 0` an English-sounding name (Type 0). Outcome `callback` is binary. 

```{r setup, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
required <- c("dplyr", "estimatr", "knitr", "broom")
missing <- setdiff(required, rownames(installed.packages()))
if (length(missing)) install.packages(missing, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")
library(dplyr)
library(estimatr)
library(knitr)
```

```{r load-data}
if (!file.exists("cleaned data.Rda")) {
  stop("Run cleaned_data.Rmd first, or put cleaned data.Rda in this working directory.")
}
loaded <- load("cleaned data.Rda")
stopifnot("df_int1" %in% loaded)
required_cols <- c("D", "callback", "firmid", "fall_data", "type",
                   "language_skills", "extracurricular_skills", "same_exp",
                   "female", "ba_quality", "ma", "exp_highquality")
stopifnot(all(required_cols %in% names(df_int1)))
dat <- df_int1 %>% mutate(
  D = as.numeric(as.character(D)),
  callback = as.numeric(as.character(callback)),
  wave = factor(fall_data)
)
stopifnot(all(na.omit(dat$D) %in% 0:1),
          all(na.omit(dat$callback) %in% 0:1))
cat("Observations:", nrow(dat), "\n")

#count under D = 0 and D = 1
print(table(dat$D, useNA = "ifany"))

#Firm count 
cat("Firms:", dplyr::n_distinct(dat$firmid), "\n")
```

The missingness-by-wave breakdown was verified in the cleaning script and will not be reproduced here. The following chunk will be to code the samples for each interaction regression. 

```{r sample-definitions}
moderators <- c("language_skills", "extracurricular_skills", "same_exp")
moderator_waves <- list(
  language_skills = c(0, 1, 2),
  extracurricular_skills = c(0, 1, 2),
  same_exp = c(0, 1)
)

# Defining control sets (covariates to held constant)
# Include only controls observed in all waves used for each model.
# reference, accreditation, legal: excluded (missing in Waves 0 and 1).
# same_exp: one of the moderators but excluded from the full-wave models (missing in Wave 2).
moderator_controls <- list(
  language_skills = c("extracurricular_skills", "female",
                      "ba_quality", "ma", "exp_highquality"),
  extracurricular_skills = c("language_skills", "female",
                             "ba_quality", "ma", "exp_highquality"),
  same_exp = c("language_skills", "extracurricular_skills", "female",
               "ba_quality", "ma", "exp_highquality")
)

moderator_samples <- setNames(lapply(moderators, function(x) {
  dat %>%
    filter(fall_data %in% moderator_waves[[x]]) %>%
    mutate(wave = droplevels(wave))
}), moderators)

sample_summary <- bind_rows(lapply(moderators, function(x) {
  s <- moderator_samples[[x]]
  data.frame(moderator = x,
             waves = paste(moderator_waves[[x]], collapse = ", "),
             n = nrow(s),
             firm_clusters = n_distinct(s$firmid),
             n_x0 = sum(s[[x]] == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
             n_x1 = sum(s[[x]] == 1, na.rm = TRUE))
}))
kable(sample_summary, caption = "Moderator-specific estimation samples")
```

# 3. Baseline average treatment effect

We estimate a wave-adjusted linear probability model:

$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \delta_t + \varepsilon_i
$$

Here, $\beta_1$ represents the average effect of an immigrant-sounding name on callback probability, controlling for wave fixed effects. This wave-adjusted specification is our baseline ATE estimate, with standard errors clustered by `firmid` using CR2.
```{r baseline-ate}
# Estimate wave-adjusted ATE
ate_wave <- lm_robust(
  callback ~ D + wave,
  data = dat,
  clusters = firmid,
  se_type = "CR2"
)

# Extract treatment effect and inference statistics
results <- broom::tidy(ate_wave, conf.int = TRUE)
treatment <- results[results$term == "D", ]

ate_table <- data.frame(
  estimate = treatment$estimate,
  se = treatment$std.error,
  ci_low = treatment$conf.low,
  ci_high = treatment$conf.high,
  n = nobs(ate_wave),
  firm_clusters = n_distinct(dat$firmid)
)

knitr::kable(
  ate_table,
  digits = 4,
  col.names = c(
    "Treatment effect", "SE", "CI lower", "CI upper",
    "N", "Firm clusters"
  ),
  caption = "Average Immigrant-Name Treatment Effect"
)
```
The estimated average treatment effect indicates that resumes with immigrant-sounding names receive callbacks at a rate 4.43 percentage points lower than those with English-sounding names, adjusted for wave fixed effects. This effect is statistically significant at the 5% level, with a 95% confidence interval of [−0.0579, −0.0307].


Note: Our extension uses firm-clustered CR2 standard errors to account for potential dependence between multiple resumes submitted to the same employer. Unlike Oreopoulos (2011), which uses heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors, our approach accounts for potential within-firm correlation. This affects the standard errors but not the OLS point estimates for an otherwise identical specification.
```{r hc1-vs-cr2}
# Comparison bwt using HC1 and CR2
model_HC1 <- lm_robust(callback ~ D + wave, data = dat, se_type = "HC1")
model_CR2 <- lm_robust(callback ~ D + wave, data = dat,
                       clusters = firmid, se_type = "CR2")
data.frame(method = c("HC1", "CR2"),
           estimate = c(coef(model_HC1)["D"], coef(model_CR2)["D"]),
           SE = c(model_HC1$std.error["D"], model_CR2$std.error["D"]))
```

# 4. Three ex-ante interaction regressions

For each moderator $X$, we estimate the following linear probability model:

$$
Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 D_i + \beta_2 X_i + \beta_3(D_i \times X_i) + \gamma'Z_i + \delta_{w(i)} + \varepsilon_i
$$

The three regressions use the moderator-specific estimation samples and control sets defined in Section 2. Here, $\beta_1$ represents the immigrant-name effect when $X=0$, $\beta_2$ captures the effect of the moderator when $D=0$, and $\beta_3$ tests whether the immigrant-name effect differs between $X=1$ and $X=0$.

```{r fit-interactions}
# Estimate the three moderator-specific interaction regressions

fit_interaction <- function(x) {

  controls <- moderator_controls[[x]]

  rhs <- c(
    "D",
    x,
    paste0("D:", x),
    controls,
    "wave"
  )

  f <- reformulate(rhs, response = "callback")

  lm_robust(
    f,
    data = moderator_samples[[x]],
    clusters = firmid,
    se_type = "CR2"
  )
}

models <- setNames(
  lapply(moderators, fit_interaction),
  moderators
)
```

```{r interaction-table}
# Extract interaction coefficients (beta_3) from each regression
interaction_table <- bind_rows(lapply(moderators, function(x) {

  m <- models[[x]]
  term <- paste0("D:", x)

  results <- broom::tidy(m, conf.int = TRUE)
  interaction <- results[results$term == term, ]

  if (nrow(interaction) != 1) {
    stop(paste("Interaction term not found:", term))
  }

  data.frame(
    moderator = x,
    beta3 = interaction$estimate,
    se = interaction$std.error,
    ci_low = interaction$conf.low,
    ci_high = interaction$conf.high,
    p_value = interaction$p.value,
    waves = paste(moderator_waves[[x]], collapse = ", "),
    n = nobs(m),
    firm_clusters = n_distinct(moderator_samples[[x]]$firmid)
  )
}))

knitr::kable(
  interaction_table,
  digits = 4,
  col.names = c(
    "Moderator", "β₃", "SE", "CI Lower", "CI Upper",
    "p-value", "Waves", "N", "Firm clusters"
  ),
  caption = "Ex-ante interaction regression results"
)
```

The results provide limited evidence of heterogeneity across the three pre-specified moderators. Language skills have a negative interaction coefficient (−0.0144), contrary to our hypothesis, but the estimate is not statistically significant (p = 0.4715). Extracurricular activities have a positive interaction coefficient (0.0307), suggesting a smaller immigrant-name penalty when extracurricular activities are listed. However, this effect is only significant at the 10% level (p = 0.0939). Multinational firm experience also has a positive interaction coefficient (0.0289), but the estimate is not statistically significant (p = 0.1912).

*Overall, none of the three interaction coefficients is statistically significant at the 5% level.* Hence, the ex-ante regressions do not provide strong evidence that these resume characteristics systematically moderate the immigrant-name penalty. The subsequent subgroup treatment-effect analysis examines the magnitude and uncertainty of the implied name penalty for X=0 and X=1.

# 5. Regression-implied subgroup treatment effects

For each binary moderator, the regression-implied subgroup treatment effects are:

$$
\hat{\tau}(X=0) = \hat{\beta}_1, \qquad
\hat{\tau}(X=1) = \hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_3
$$

For $X=1$, the variance accounts for the covariance between $\hat{\beta}_1$ and $\hat{\beta}_3$:

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1 + \hat{\beta}_3)
= \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\beta}_1)
+ \operatorname{Var}(\hat{\beta}_3)
+ 2\operatorname{Cov}(\hat{\beta}_1,\hat{\beta}_3)
$$
```{r subgroup effects}
subgroup_effects <- bind_rows(lapply(moderators, function(x) {
  m <- models[[x]]
  s <- moderator_samples[[x]]
  b <- coef(m)
  V <- vcov(m)
  interaction <- paste0("D:", x)
  out <- lapply(0:1, function(z) {
    a <- setNames(rep(0, length(b)), names(b))
    a["D"] <- 1
    if (z == 1) a[interaction] <- 1
    estimate <- sum(a * b)
    se <- sqrt(drop(t(a) %*% V %*% a))
    # Conservative approximation using available coefficient-specific CR2 df.
    # The exact contrast-specific small-sample df may differ.
    involved <- if (z == 0) "D" else c("D", interaction)
    df <- min(m$df[match(involved, names(b))], na.rm = TRUE)
    crit <- qt(0.975, df = df)
    data.frame(moderator = x, subgroup = paste0("X=", z),
               estimate = estimate, se = se,
               ci_low = estimate - crit * se,
               ci_high = estimate + crit * se,
               n_subgroup = sum(s[[x]] == z),
               firm_clusters_subgroup = n_distinct(s$firmid[s[[x]] == z]))
  })
  bind_rows(out)
}))
knitr::kable(
  subgroup_effects,
  digits = 4,
  col.names = c(
    "Moderator", "Subgroup", "Treatment effect",
    "SE", "CI lower", "CI upper",
    "N", "Firm clusters"
  ),
  caption = "Estimated Immigrant-Name Treatment Effects by Subgroups"
)
```

The subgroup treatment effects estimated from the interaction regressions will be compared with corresponding subgroup average treatment effects (ATEs) estimated using the causal forest. Both approaches will use the same subgroup definitions and target observations to ensure comparability. Specifically, the comparison for multinational firm experience will be restricted to Waves 0 and 1, while the other two moderators will use all three waves. The comparison will focus on the direction, magnitude and uncertainty of the estimated treatment effects.
